summary: Defines how the X.500 Directory can be used to support routing in the Message Handling System, mapping an O/R address to the next message transfer agent that is nearer the destination. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how X.400 mail systems can look up their next hop in an X.500 directory. It organizes routing information by recipient address and allows multiple routing trees and alternate MTAs.

questions: how does x.500 support x.400 routing
what is a routing tree in x.400
what is a routing tree in x.500
subtitle: An experimental design for using X.500 directory data to route X.400 mail.

tldr.problem: Administrators had to build and maintain complex routing tables for X.400 message handling, making global routing difficult to manage.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC stores routing trees in the X.500 Directory. An MTA maps a recipient's O/R Address into the tree and selects a next-hop MTA from the available routing information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1801 describes an experimental, directory-based approach and states that its security issues are not discussed in the memo.

today: RFC 1801 is an Experimental RFC published in June 1995. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Routing Problem
sections.content:
Message Handling System routing chooses the next Message Transfer Agent (MTA) on the path to a recipient. The sender starts with the recipient's O/R Address and repeats the lookup until the message can be delivered to the user agent.

The RFC aims to make routing easier to manage, support alternate routes and different protocols, and scale to a global network. It describes a longer-term Directory-based approach, distinct from an interim table-based method.
sections.plainLanguage: Each MTA needs to know which MTA should receive a message next. This RFC proposes storing that information in a shared directory instead of hand-maintained tables.

sections.title: Direct Routes and Communities
sections.content:
Direct connections reduce delay and avoid relay points, but relays can support charge arrangements, copy delivery, format conversion, protocol conversion, and a single external entry point for an organization. The RFC therefore supports both direct and indirect routing.

It groups routing information into communities: a public open community, a private local community, hierarchical communities such as an organization, and closed groups of MTAs that agree to route among themselves. An MTA can publish and look up services in more than one community.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can go directly to an MTA or pass through a relay. Communities define which routing information is public, local, hierarchical, or shared by an agreed group.

sections.title: Routing Trees in X.500
sections.content:
Each community is represented by a routing tree in the X.500 Directory. The open community tree starts at the directory root; other trees can be rooted elsewhere. To search, an MTA maps the O/R Address to a distinguished name, adds the routing-tree root, and reads that name from the directory.

Directory entries can list next-hop MTAs, route weights, filters for parts of an address, and actions to take when no MTA can be used. The MTA keeps an ordered list of routing trees, so private routes can be checked before the open tree or a default route.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory follows the structure of recipient addresses. An MTA looks up the address in its selected routing trees to find a next hop.

sections.title: Selecting an MTA
sections.content:
Within a routing tree, the algorithm finds the longest matching address and then considers parent entries. A route weight ranges from 0 to 20, with lower values preferred. The RFC gives 0 for direct delivery, 5 for a preferred MTA, and 10 for a backup; equal weights allow a random choice.

Before selecting an MTA, the routing process checks whether it supports a usable protocol and transport community and whether capability, policy, and authentication requirements allow the transfer. The RFC says a routing decision can be configured to use as few as two directory reads.
sections.plainLanguage: The MTA checks the most specific matching route first and can move to less specific entries if needed. Lower route weights are preferred, but an MTA must also meet protocol and policy requirements.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security-considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Security-related requirements appear in the routing design, including MTA authentication requirements and bilateral agreements.

The document does not provide a separate security analysis or define a security mechanism for the directory-based routing approach.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says it does not discuss security issues. It mentions authentication requirements as part of routing decisions but gives no security analysis.
